title: mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya sutta
credit: Pāḷi text and English translation as in Mor’s Pāḷi Workshop booklet.

paras.en: “… On seeing a visual form with the eye, he is not infatuated with it if it is pleasing; he is not repelled by it if it is unpleasing. He abides with awareness of the body established, with an unlimited mind,
and he understands as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those bad unwholesome states cease without remainder.

Having thus abandoned attraction and repulsion,
whatever vedanā he feels, whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he does not delight in that vedanā, embrace it, or remain holding to it.
As he does not do so, delight in vedanā ceases in him.

On hearing a sound with the ear…
On smelling an odor with the nose…
On tasting a flavor with the tongue…
On experiencing a sensation with the body…

On cognizing a mental object with the mind,
he is not infatuated with it if it is pleasing;
he is not repelled by it if it is unpleasing.
He abides with awareness of the body established,
with an unlimited mind, and he understands as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those bad unwholesome states cease without remainder.

Having thus abandoned attraction and repulsion,
whatever vedanā he feels, whether pleasant or painful
or neither-painful-nor-pleasant,
he does not delight in that vedanā,
embrace it, or remain holding to it.
As he does not do so, delight in vedanā ceases in him.

With the cessation of his delight comes cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and misery cease.
Such is the cessation of this whole mass of dukkha.”
